assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm heterogeneity and selection changed how trade is modelled. The framework explains who exports, how gains from trade arise through reallocation, and why intra-industry trade matters. It reshaped theory, empirics and policy analysis, and it extends the earlier new-trade-theory recognition.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) supplies the canonical heterogeneous-firm model with selection into exporting. Helpman contributed the broader monopolistic-competition and firm-level trade framework and the empirical follow-ups. Redding's quantitative and spatial extensions are very influential, but the core idea is cleanly attributable to the two proposed names.
assessment.maturity: More than two decades of confirmation across many datasets, countries and structural applications. The idea has long been standard textbook material, so the timing is ripe.
uncertainties: Whether the committee would prefer to include Redding or a co-author such as Bernard and Jensen for the empirical facts on exporter premia, which are not in the credited list.
Helpman also appears in another trade-policy entry, so the committee may weigh how to divide credit across his work.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Showed how collateral constraints create a dynamic feedback between asset prices and borrowing capacity, amplifying and propagating small shocks into large credit cycles. This is a foundational mechanism in macro-finance and a standard element of crisis and policy analysis.
assessment.attribution: The 1997 Kiyotaki–Moore model is the identifiable origin of the mechanism, with a clear two-person credit. Gertler and Gilchrist are important for the financial accelerator and its empirical side, but the 2022 prize already recognised related financial-intermediation work, so the core credit is more tightly attributable to the two.
assessment.maturity: Nearly three decades of influence, with extensive confirmation after the 2008 crisis in theory, quantitative models and empirical work on collateral channels.
uncertainties: Overlap with the financial-accelerator literature (Bernanke–Gertler) and with the 2022 prize may reduce perceived novelty.
Direct causal tests of the collateral channel are indirect, and the theory is stylised.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The New Keynesian framework, with nominal rigidities, microfounded Phillips curves and rule-based monetary policy, underlies modern central-bank analysis and inflation targeting. Its practical and intellectual influence is very large.
assessment.attribution: Credit is spread over many contributors: Calvo (price-setting), Taylor (staggered contracts and the policy rule), Woodford (the integrated framework), Gali (the textbook formulation and empirics), and Christiano–Eichenbaum (medium-scale estimated models). Three names is a tight selection, and any three omit major contributors.
assessment.maturity: Three decades of use in policy institutions, with the framework tested and revised through the financial crisis and the post-pandemic inflation episode.
uncertainties: Attribution is the main obstacle: several comparably important contributors would be excluded.
The framework's performance on inflation dynamics after 2021 and its limitations in the financial crisis are still debated.
The 2022 monetary and financial prize is adjacent in subject.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Combined credible empirical designs with a task-based view of technology and trade to show how import competition and automation reshape local labour markets, wages and political outcomes. It has had wide influence on research and public debate, and it speaks to the broader themes of technological change and distributional consequences.
assessment.attribution: The China-shock evidence is attributable to Autor, Dorn and Hanson. The wider task-based and skill-bias literature involves Katz, Levy and Murnane, and Acemoglu and Restrepo, so credit for the full field is shared more widely than the three names.
assessment.maturity: A decade or more of work, with replications and extensions across countries. Some long-run persistence results are still developing.
uncertainties: The task-model origins sit partly outside the credited names, and Katz's link to earlier recognition complicates the group.
Recent prizes on labour markets (2021) and on technology and growth (2025) may weigh on timing.
The magnitude of the China shock's net welfare effect is contested.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Showed quantitatively that misallocation of inputs across firms can explain a large share of cross-country income gaps. This offers a micro-founded account of productivity differences that connects growth, development and industrial policy. It generated a large literature with a new set of measurement tools.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh–Klenow (2009) is the central empirical paper, and Restuccia–Rogerson (2008) is its theoretical companion. Choosing two names leaves out Restuccia and Rogerson, so credit is divisible but not clean.
assessment.maturity: Fifteen or more years of application, including replications across many countries. Measurement criticisms have been raised and partly addressed.
uncertainties: Results are sensitive to measurement error and to the specification of firm-level distortions.
Whether the committee sees this as one discovery or a family of related contributions, and who would be included.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The alternating-offers model gave bargaining a tractable non-cooperative foundation and linked it to market outcomes, which connects to search, labour, and decentralised trade. It is a core piece of economic theory with durable pedagogic and applied influence.
assessment.attribution: Rubinstein's 1982 paper is the clear origin. Rubinstein–Wolinsky extends it to markets. Binmore's contributions are important for interpretation and the Nash-program connection, but are secondary on discovery.
assessment.maturity: More than forty years of use, and the model is fully established. Prize timing is not a constraint on maturity, though related game-theory work has been recognised.
uncertainties: Theory with limited direct empirical testing, so impact is mostly conceptual.
Competing priority claims and extensions (for example Stahl, and Binmore–Rubinstein–Wolinsky) could complicate attribution.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Built the modern framework for analysing how electoral rules, constitutions and state capacity shape fiscal policy and public goods provision. It combines formal theory with comparative empirical tests and covers both advanced and developing economies.
assessment.attribution: Persson and Tabellini are the main authors of the constitutional and electoral-rules programme. Besley's work on state capacity and political agency is closely related and shares credit. The three together form a coherent group.
assessment.maturity: Developed across more than twenty-five years, with empirical confirmation across countries. The 2024 prize on institutions and prosperity is adjacent and may affect timing.
uncertainties: Causal identification of constitutional effects is difficult, and some cross-country results have been questioned.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Used granular household and regional data to show how credit expansion, household leverage and debt overhang drive booms, busts and weak recoveries. This shifted macroeconomic attention to household balance sheets and distributional channels.
assessment.attribution: Mian and Sufi are the core authors of the household-debt research programme, and the credit is clearly theirs. Campbell's contributions lie elsewhere (asset pricing and household finance) and fit less well into this discovery.
assessment.maturity: About fifteen years of work and widely replicated, though the field is younger than the other leading entries and some conclusions are still being refined.
uncertainties: Relatively recent compared with other candidates, and some causal interpretations of credit-supply effects remain debated.
The 2022 prize on banks and financial crises is adjacent in subject.
